choices.hint: The driver's instinct points the same way the timetable does; trusting it could save you a night. It also stakes everything on one half-asleep memory, and if he's wrong you've walked hours into the wrong ward.

choices.x: Work the witnesses outward in a slow spiral instead of chasing one lead.
choices.hint: Methodical canvassing catches the contradictions a single lead would hide. It is achingly slow, and the trail cools a degree with every door, every dawn, every hour you spend being thorough.

choices.x: Stop walking and just watch one intersection he'd have to cross.
choices.hint: Patience at a chokepoint sometimes beats motion — let the city bring him to you. Or let the whole night pass at one corner while he takes a street you never imagined, and learn nothing but the look of a lamppost at four a.m.

beats.scene: A convenience store at the edge of nowhere, the small economy of asking strangers for help
prose: There is a particular kind of person awake at this hour in a konbini at the edge of a residential ward — the night clerk who has seen everything and judges none of it, the salaryman drinking canned coffee to delay going home, the old woman buying flowers for a grave she'll visit at dawn. You come in under the white light smelling of rain and roads and you have to decide, fast, how much of the truth a stranger will hold for you. Too little and they shrug; too much and they back away from the kind of trouble that follows a sibling looking for a sibling at four in the morning during the festival of the dead. The slow road runs on these small transactions, and you are learning their exchange rate the hard way.

The clerk is younger than you expected and he looks at the photo of Gin a long time before he says anything, and when he speaks it is not what you wanted but it is true, which on this road is the only currency that compounds. He's seen the man. Not tonight — two nights ago, and again last week, the same man, always northbound, always with the slightly wrong walk of someone being steered, and once with a second person who the clerk can't quite describe, except that being near them made the cold drinks case hum in a way he'd reported to maintenance twice. You stand in the fluorescent hum and feel the braid of it: your brother, more than once, on a route, with a passenger the ordinary eye can only register as a malfunction. The slow road has just told you something no faster road would have stopped to hear — that this isn't a kidnapping, it's a routine.

You buy something you don't need, because that is how this economy works, and the clerk tells you one more thing while he makes change: there's a woman who runs a late stall three stations up who 'keeps track of the ones who wander', who the unregistered and the half-touched go to when the official world has no slot for them. He doesn't have a name for what she does. You do — or you have a guess, and the guess is the first time tonight the supernatural has reached into your human search, not as a power you wield but as a place you might walk to. You thank him properly, the way you'd want a stranger thanked for helping look for your brother, and you go back out into the dark with one more thread and the strange warmth of having been, for two minutes, simply helped.

choices.x: Go straight to the woman who 'keeps track of the ones who wander'.
choices.hint: She may have seen Gin's route with eyes that understand it — the best lead of the night. People who track the wandering are rarely free with what they know, and you have nothing to trade but a story she's heard a hundred times.

choices.x: Press the clerk for the route's other stops before you lose him to his shift.
choices.hint: Pinning the whole pattern now means you can find Gin even if the woman won't help. It also keeps a kind young man longer in a conversation that could mark him, to whatever hums the drinks case, as someone who talked.

choices.x: Rest an hour here, eat, let your body keep up with the road.
choices.hint: You cannot walk to Kita on an empty body and a sleepless night; the road is long and you are the vehicle. Every hour of rest is an hour the routine runs without you watching it.

beats.scene: The late stall three stations north, and the people the factions never count
prose: The woman's stall is the kind of place the official world draws no line around — a few stools, a kerosene heater for a night that isn't cold, a hand-lettered menu, and a clientele that the Directorate's registries and the Tower's records have simply never managed to contain. These are the unregistered and the half-touched, the animal-mediums and the once-possessed and the people who saw something once and have organised their whole quiet lives around never seeing it again. They are exactly the people the fast roads step over, because a faction's eye slides off anyone it can't file, and you understand as you sit down among them that the slow road has brought you to the one census that might actually have your brother in it.

The woman does not perform mystery; she ladles soup and watches you decide whether to be honest. When you put Gin's photo on the counter she doesn't touch it, only looks, and then she looks at you — at your eyes, specifically, at the place behind them you have kept folded shut all night — and something in her face settles, as if she has just confirmed a suspicion she'd rather have been wrong about. 'You're his,' she says. 'The one who could look and won't.' It is not a question and it is not an accusation, but it lands like both, and around you the quiet clientele go a degree quieter, the way a room does when someone says the true thing out loud. She has seen Gin. She has seen, she tells you, what walks in his steps. And she has been counting how many of her people have gone north and not come back, the way you count anything you can't stop.

What she gives you is not a location but a shape, and it is worse for being a shape: the northbound ones, the wanderers, the half-touched who drift up the Kita line and thin out of her count — they aren't being taken at random. They're being gathered. Someone up there has been, in her flat word, 'tidying' — collecting the loose, the unregistered, the bright-but-unguarded, the way you'd sweep filings toward a magnet. Your brother is part of the tidying and also, she thinks, doing some of it, his familiar warmth used to make the gathering gentle, a known face to lead the unknown north. 'The Healer,' she says, and the word in her mouth is not a title, it's a diagnosis. 'He doesn't take. He invites. That's why none of your factions have a file thick enough to stop it. You can't arrest an invitation.'

choices.x: Ask her to point you at the next person scheduled to 'wander' north.
choices.hint: Following the next invitation in real time could walk you straight to the gathering point. It means using a stranger as bait on a road you swore would cost no one but you.

choices.x: Ask instead what the gathered ones have in common — find the pattern, not the path.
choices.hint: Understanding who gets invited might tell you why Gin was, and what the Healer is building toward. Pattern is slower than pursuit, and the soup-stall's heater won't keep the trail warm while you think.

choices.x: Show her you trust her — let the fold come loose, just once, just for her to see.
choices.hint: Opening the registers a hair would prove you're truly Gin's and might earn you everything she knows. It is the first crack in the one rule that has kept you human all night, and cracks on this road do not reseal.

beats.scene: Northbound at dawn with no one behind you, and the cost of refusing the fast lanes comes due
prose: Dawn finds you on a Kita-bound platform with the festival burning down to its embers, the lanterns guttering, the dead presumably gone home, and your feet a single continuous ache that has stopped being information and become just the weather of your body. This is the hour the road bills you for everything you refused. A faction would have driven you here. The Gift would have flown you. You walked, and the walking has spent a whole night and most of your strength to bring you only to the edge of the place the others would have started from, and you feel the unfairness of it the way you feel the cold rail under your hands — flatly, without anyone to appeal to. No one is behind you. No procedure protects you. If the thing wearing Gin turns and notices the tired person on the platform, there is no one you can call who will come.

And it does notice — not the way the Gift would be noticed, with the seat's cold eye opening, but in the small, human, deniable way the slow road is haunted: a man across the platform who is reading you a beat too long, a station attendant whose helpfulness has one wrong edge, a sense, unprovable, that the routine you've been tracing has begun, lazily, to trace you back. This is the road's particular dread. It cannot show you a monster, so it shows you the possibility of one in every ordinary face, and leaves you no sight to confirm or dismiss it. You have made yourself into exactly one thing all night — a person asking after Gin — and you are far enough up the line now that asking has become a way of announcing yourself to whatever is doing the gathering.

You could still buy speed, even here, even now. There is always a faster road available to someone desperate enough at dawn — a payphone number the soup-woman slipped you that rings a Grid fixer, a Directorate poster on the platform wall with a tip line that would put a car and a badge behind you within the hour, the simple final option of unfolding your eyes and burning the rest of the distance. The whole night has been a refusal of these, and the refusal has gotten you here intact and unnoticed and nearly out of road. The question the platform asks, while the man across the way folds and unfolds his newspaper, is whether intact and unnoticed is worth the last hour you may have before a lucid window in your brother closes for good.

choices.x: Hold the line — stay slow, stay human, ride the last stretch as just a passenger.
choices.hint: Refuse speed one final time and you arrive the way you set out: unread, unowned, yourself. You may also arrive too late, and spend the rest of your life knowing exactly which trains you let pass.

choices.x: Make the one call — the Grid fixer, a single fast favour at the very end.
choices.hint: One ride from a fixer closes the distance before the window shuts. The Grid never does a favour that doesn't become a handle, and you'd be handing it the thing you walked all night to keep.

choices.x: Confront the man with the newspaper — force the ordinary dread to declare itself.
choices.hint: Making the watcher show his hand ends the not-knowing that's eating you. If he's nothing, you've burned time and nerve; if he's something, you've started a fight with no faction at your back and no sight to fight with.

beats.scene: The fast lane, refused: a CVD junior offers you a car, a badge, and a name to fill in
prose: They come for the unaffiliated last, because the unaffiliated are the hardest to find, and the irony of it nearly makes you laugh as the unmarked car slows beside you on the Kita street and the window comes down on a young CVD officer who is trying very hard to look like help. The Directorate has been watching the gathering too — of course it has, a routine that thins the membrane is exactly the kind of thing it exists to file — and it has noticed, at the very end, the one variable its registries couldn't predict: a sibling tracking the whole pattern on foot, with no faction, no Gift signature, no file. You are, to the young officer's evident discomfort, a blank space in the records that walked itself to the centre of an active case, and the Directorate would very much like to fill the blank in.

The offer is reasonable, which is what makes it dangerous. A car for the last stretch you're too tired to walk. A badge's worth of protection for the threshold you're about to cross unarmed. Resources, backup, the apparatus of a faction that genuinely wants the membrane left alone — all of it yours, in exchange for the one thing the whole night was built to withhold: your brother's name, formally given, on the Directorate's terms, which means Gin stops being a person you're looking for and becomes a person they're processing. The junior officer says the word 'cooperation' and you hear, underneath it, the soft click of a handle being fitted to your brother. Every road but this one began by handing over that handle. You have walked all night precisely to arrive without it, and here, at the last mile, exhaustion makes the case for giving it up better than any officer could.

You look at the young officer and you can see he half hopes you'll refuse — that some part of him knows the difference between a sibling and an informant and would rather not be the one who erases it. The slow road has made you legible to the Directorate in the gentlest possible way, as a witness and not a weapon, and that legibility is itself a kind of door: walk through it and you finish the search with the whole machine behind you and your brother's name in its mouth. Stay on the pavement and you keep faith with the only principle that's gotten you this far, and you keep walking toward the thinning wall with nothing, still, but your own two feet and the warmth of a brother you refuse to spend.

choices.x: Refuse the badge and keep walking — no name, no handle, no faction.
choices.hint: Holding to the road's whole point means arriving at the wall as no one's instrument. It also means facing what's there with a tired body, no backup, and a young officer's car pulling away from the last help you'll be offered.

choices.x: Take the ride but not the deal — accept the car, refuse to give the name.
choices.hint: Bargaining for the distance without paying in Gin's name is the cleverest play available. The Directorate does not give half-favours, and a debt left vague at dawn is a debt they get to define later.

choices.x: Give the officer everything — the routine, the soup-woman's count, the Healer.
choices.hint: Handing the Directorate the full pattern arms the one faction that wants the membrane saved. It also turns every person who helped you tonight into a line in a file, and your brother into a case the machine now owns.

beats.scene: The last streets to the wall, the trail made entirely of small human things
prose: The final approach to the thinning wall is, on this road, the strangest part, because you arrive at it not by sight and not by procedure but by the sheer mass of small things you have carried up the Kita line all night. A clerk's memory of a humming cooler. A cab driver's word for the direction of a calling. A soup-woman's tally of the vanished. A timetable folded to a single stop. Laid end to end, the ordinary facts have become a line as straight and certain as anything the Gift could draw, and you walk it into a quiet northern neighbourhood where the wrongness, when you finally reach it, is not visible at all — it is felt, the way you feel a held breath in a house, the way the dawn light here seems to arrive a half-second late, as if it had to come a little further than light should have to.

You understand, walking these last streets, that the slow road has given you the one thing the fast roads never could: you know how the gathering was done, because you retraced it at the speed it was done at. You know it was gentle. You know it wore a familiar face. You know the people it took were the uncounted, the ones no faction would miss, and you know your brother's warmth was the bait that made the leaving feel like being led home. None of this is sight. All of it is understanding, accumulated on foot, and it has brought you to the threshold with a map of the crime drawn entirely in human testimony — admissible nowhere, true everywhere, and yours alone.

And then, in the late-arriving light, you see him. Not a residue, not a braid of pressures — Gin, your brother, standing at the place where the air comes a half-second late, ordinary as anything, waiting at a thinned wall the way a person waits at a bus stop, his familiar warmth doing the patient work of making a monstrous place look like somewhere it's safe to gather. He has not seen you yet. You have walked all night to be a person finding a person, and here at the end the road has kept its promise exactly: you have found him, with your own tired eyes, paying only in time and shoe leather and the steady refusal to become anything that would have gotten you here faster. The cost was that it took all night. The gift is that you arrive as yourself, unread, with nothing behind you and nothing owed, and a clear human sight of your brother before he turns.

choices.x: Call his name across the quiet street — reach him as a person, out loud.
choices.hint: A voice he's known his whole life might surface the real Gin faster than any power. It also announces you, plainly, to the patient thing wearing him, in the one place it has worked hardest to keep quiet.

choices.x: Watch first — learn what he's doing here before you let yourself be seen.
choices.hint: A few minutes of observation might show you the mechanism of the gathering and how to break it. Every minute is a minute closer to whatever the half-late light is waiting for, and to losing the cover of being unnoticed.

choices.x: Close the distance quietly and put a hand on him before he can turn.
choices.hint: Touch is the most human argument you have, and the hardest for a passenger to answer. Reaching a thinned wall and laying hands on the bait is also exactly the proximity the Healer's whole gentle routine was built to produce.

beats.scene: The threshold, reached by the long way, where being no one is the only card you hold
prose: You arrive at the wall the way only this road could deliver you — with nothing. No badge to flash, no favour to call in, no register flung open to read the seam entire. The other roads converge here too, each handing you a different instrument and a different price already paid; you converge here empty-handed, and for a vertiginous moment the emptiness feels like the failure the whole night was secretly building toward. The membrane has been worked thin in front of you, lovingly, by someone who calls thinning a healing, and you cannot read the plan off it the way the Gift would. You can only stand where your feet have brought you and understand it the slow way: that this is where the gathered ones were gathered, that the vacant Thirteenth Seat is the magnet the soup-woman's filings were swept toward, that your brother's warmth has been the kindness that made a culling feel like a homecoming.

But the road has been building you a different weapon all night, and you feel it now as the last thing it gives you: you are, to the thing on the other side of the wall, illegible. The Gift would have made you the brightest object in northern Tokyo, a flare fired at the opening eye. The factions would have made you a known quantity, a file the Healer could have read in advance. You are neither. You are a tired person who walked here on testimony and stubbornness, carrying no signature anything can lock onto, and at the threshold of a place built to collect the bright and the registered, being no one at all turns out to be the one approach the trap was never designed to catch. The seat's cold attention sweeps the wall and finds nothing to fix on, because you brought nothing for it to fix on, and in that blind spot you are still, impossibly, free to move.

And then his familiar warmth finds you — not flung across a seam by the Gift, but simply Gin, close enough now to feel you the human way, and for one window the size of a held breath the passenger is asleep or distracted or outvoted and it is only your brother, lucid and horrified to see you here. He does not tell you you're too bright; on this road there is no brightness to warn against. He tells you the other thing, the worse and truer thing, in the only language the wall leaves him: that he can't stop walking north, that the kindness in him is being used as bait, that he had hoped no one would ever come the long way and find him doing it. You have found him as yourself, unread, unowned, with nothing behind you and nothing owed — and the only question the wall leaves is what a person with no instrument but their own two hands and their own real face does, now, at the thinned edge of the place their brother is being used to fill.

choices.x: Answer him as his sibling — no plan, no power, just the truth between you.
choices.hint: The one thing the Healer's gentle routine can't counterfeit is the real history between you and Gin. Spent here, at the wall, it might wake the man inside the bait — or it might be the last lucid window you ever get, used up on a conversation instead of a rescue.

choices.x: Stay illegible and try to walk him out the way you walked in — quietly, as nobody.
choices.hint: Leading Gin back down the line as two unremarkable people might slip you both past the seat's blind attention. The thing wearing him does not have to stay asleep, and the long road home is long, and you have no faction to catch you if it wakes.

choices.x: Refuse to take a side at the wall — hold the threshold, change nothing, just stay with him.
choices.hint: Refusing to act, here, keeps every ending still possible and keeps you human to the last. It also leaves the membrane thinning, the seat waiting, and your brother walking north — and someday the not-choosing becomes a choice the city made for you.

sideMissions.title: Yua's Debt
sideMissions.hook: A street kid who watches out for Rei owes the wrong people; the favour she calls in is smaller and worse than money.

beats.scene: Yanaka, the third night of Obon, where the lantern-sellers thin out
prose: Yua finds you the way she always has — not by walking up but by already being there, a smudge of a girl in a man's outgrown jacket leaning on the cold side of a vending machine where the festival light doesn't reach. She is fourteen, or says she is, and she has watched the back of your neck on more platforms than you have ever thanked her for. Tonight the Obon lanterns are going down the Yanaka slope toward the river, paper boats for the dead finding their way home, and she will not look at them. I'm not asking for money, she says before you can offer it, fast, like a thing rehearsed against the chance she'd lose her nerve. Money I could've got. This is the other kind.

You have known for a year that Yua owes someone on the Grid, the way you know a tooth is going bad — by the way she favours one side of every conversation, by the appointments she keeps that she will not name. Now she pulls her sleeve up past the wrist and shows you the underside of her forearm, where there is no mark at all, only skin, and that is the wrong thing, that is the frightening thing: there should be a memory there and there is a smooth absence instead, the place where one has already been lifted clean. I borrowed against remembering, she says. I didn't have anything else worth holding. And the last payment comes due tonight, while the gate's open, because that's when it's cheapest for them and dearest for me.

She tells you the rest in the flat voice children use for the worst things, because feeling it would cost more than she has. The collateral on the final note is the only clear memory she has left of her brother Haru — his actual face, not the photograph she has worn soft, the real grain of his voice telling her something on a train. When the Tallyman collects tonight it comes out of her like a tooth and she will keep the shape of the loss without the thing that was lost. I can't stop it, she says. But you've got two registers you keep stuffed down where they don't show. So I'm asking you to stand there when they take it, and let me tell it to you first — so it's somewhere. So Haru's somewhere. That's the whole favour. It's smaller than money. I know it's worse.

choices.x: "Tell me now, before we go anywhere. I'll hold it."
choices.hint: Taking a memory into a suppressed register isn't free filing — it weights the register, and a register that wakes up on a borrowed grief wakes up loud. You'd be carrying her brother and tipping your own hand at once.

choices.x: "We're not paying it in memory. Take me to whoever holds the note."
choices.hint: The Grid does not renegotiate for sentiment, and a broker who deals in remembering can read what you'd offer instead off the back of your eyes. You'd be walking in with the one currency you can't afford to be seen carrying.

choices.x: "How long until they collect? Don't lie to me about the time."
choices.hint: She has been managing you the way she manages everyone who might help — by the slice. Push for the truth and you'll learn the window is shorter than she let on, and that she came to you last, not first.

beats.scene: Below the Sendagi crossing, where the Grid keeps a night-market the registered city can't see
prose: The Tallyman does not have a face so much as the place where keeping accounts has worn one away. It works a stall under the Sendagi tracks that you would walk past a hundred times registered and never once see, and the moment Yua steps under its awning the festival noise overhead goes muffled, as though the whole bright living city has been folded behind glass. There are jars on its shelves, hundreds, and you make yourself not look too long at any one of them because each holds a little weather of light that moves like something remembering being alive. The watcher girl brings a witness, it says, and its attention crosses your skin like a hand checking a coat for the shape of a wallet. Two of them. One folded twice. How thoughtful, to bring me the interest along with the principal.

It lays the note on the counter the way a doctor lays out an instrument, and the terms are written in Yua's own hand from a year ago, a child's careful characters promising what a child shouldn't have to weigh. The memory of Haru's face, in exchange for the rent she could not make the winter she was eleven. It has been good to her, the Tallyman points out, almost gently — it could have called sooner, on a colder night, for less reason. It is calling now, during Obon, because remembering runs thin when the dead are walking and a memory comes loose easier through the gap, and a debt should be collected at the season that serves the creditor. Unless, it says, and lets the word hang, the witness would prefer to be the payer. I am not particular about whose remembering I file. Only that the ledger closes tonight.

You feel both registers turn over at once, the way a dog lifts its head at a sound under the floor — they have caught the smell of the jars, of so much remembering held still, and they want it. That is the trap inside the trap, and Yua does not know to warn you of it: this is exactly the kind of place that could wake the thing you have spent your whole life keeping asleep. The Tallyman watches you the way it watches everything, as an amount. You came in carrying so much, it says. It would be such a small adjustment, to leave a little lighter.

choices.x: Offer one of your own memories in Haru's place — a thing of yours, freely given.
choices.hint: A clean substitution closes Yua's note and saves Haru's face. But you choose what you offer, and grief makes you reach for the heaviest thing in the room to prove you mean it — and the heaviest thing you own is a morning in a kitchen with Gin, which you cannot afford to lose and may not be able to keep yourself from offering.

choices.x: Refuse the terms and ask what the note would take instead of memory — a service, a name, a debt deferred.
choices.hint: The Tallyman keeps every kind of ledger. It will name a price that isn't memory — and the alternative currencies it deals in are favours owed into the Grid, the same web Gin disappeared through. You'd be trading Yua's grief for a thread that ties you to the thing you're hunting.

choices.x: Let the collection happen, and catch the memory into your register as it comes loose — the favour she actually asked for.
choices.hint: This is the smaller, worse thing she wanted: not rescue, just survival of the memory somewhere. It takes Haru out of her anyway. And the register you open to catch him is one you have never once chosen to open on purpose — you don't know what else comes through the door you hold ajar.

beats.scene: The collection — the instrument set, the gate at its widest
prose: Whatever you decided, the moment of collection is the same shape, and it is quiet, and that is the horror of it — you keep waiting for it to be violent and it is only precise. The Tallyman does not reach for Yua so much as ask the memory a question it cannot help answering, and you watch the girl's face go through something no face should have to do in front of a witness: a brief, terrible brightening, as Haru comes all the way up to the surface one last time to be counted, the real him, laughing at something on a train with the specific crooked tooth the photograph never kept. For one second Yua is eleven and not alone. Then the second ends.

If you reached, you feel him cross — a stranger's brother arriving in a room of yourself you keep dark, the weight of a love you did not earn settling into a register that shudders at the unfamiliar grief and threatens, for one long swimming instant, to open the rest of the way and let out whatever else lives behind it. If you paid, you feel the gap where your own given thing used to be, already smoothing over, already becoming a loss without an edge. If you let it go to close the ledger clean, you watch the brightness leave her and you understand that you chose the cheapest door and that she will know, the way the watched always know about the watcher. The Tallyman files the note and the awning's muffling lifts a half-inch, festival noise leaking back in, the living city remembering it is there.

The ledger is closed, it says, and it is already looking past both of you at the next set of footsteps in the dark. But it pauses, because it deals in what people will give and it has taken your measure now and found it useful to know. You hold a great deal you have not counted, it tells you, not unkindly, the way a creditor is kind to a client it intends to see again. When you are ready to know the true sum of yourself, you know which stall keeps the longest ledger in the city. Bring the watcher girl. She remembers where the door is, even when she cannot remember why.

choices.x: Get Yua out into the lantern-light before you let yourself feel any of it.
choices.hint: She is fourteen and she has just lost the last real piece of someone, in public, in front of you. Putting her first is right — and it means you carry whatever just happened to you, alone, unexamined, into a register you can't be sure is closed again.

choices.x: Tell the Tallyman you'll be back to learn the true sum — and mean it.
choices.hint: It is the first creature in the city to offer you a straight account of what you actually are. That is a door you have wanted your whole life. It is also a hook, set by a thing that does nothing without a ledger, in the exact season your brother went looking through a gap like this one.

choices.x: Say nothing. Pick up a lantern from the stack and put it in Yua's hands.
choices.hint: A boat for a brother she can no longer picture. The gesture costs nothing and means everything, which is the only kind of payment left tonight — and it tells her you understood exactly what you witnessed, which is its own weight to have laid on a child.

beats.scene: The river stairs, after — paper boats going down toward a sea none of them will reach
prose: You take her down to the water where the others are launching their lanterns, and Yua kneels at the bottom step with the paper boat you put in her hands, and for a while she cannot light it because she has forgotten who it is for. That is the part the Tallyman charged her for and did not bother to mention: not the memory only but the why of keeping it, so that she holds a grief with the name scraped off, a love with no object, the worst kind of debt because it cannot be discharged by remembering or forgotten by trying. It was somebody, she says, testing the words. It was somebody good. I can feel the shape of good. I just can't get the rest to come. And you, who chose tonight whether to carry her brother or your own kitchen or nothing at all, sit down on the cold stone beside her and do not lie about how that feels.

If you took Haru into your register, you find you can give a little of him back — not the memory, you cannot return what the ledger took, but the fact of him, the train and the tooth and the laugh, told as a witness tells a thing, so that she has a story where she used to have the man. It is not the same and it is not nothing, and she listens to her own brother described by a stranger with a hunger that breaks something in you that you did not know was load-bearing. If you paid instead, you discover the cost only now — reaching for the thing you gave and finding the smooth place where it was, learning by its absence how much you must have loved it. If you let the collection close clean, the silence between you on the steps is honest, at least, and she does not pretend you saved her, and you do not pretend you tried.

When the boat finally goes down — and it does, all of them do, the whole grieving city pushing its dead gently out toward a darkness that is, tonight, briefly thin — Yua watches it until the current takes it round the bend and then she stands, and she is fourteen again, and the watching is already back in her, the appraisal of exits and angles that has kept her alive. You'll go looking for your one too, she says, not asking, because she has watched the back of your neck for a year and she knows the shape of a person hunting a brother through a gap in the world. When you do — don't borrow against the remembering. Whatever they offer. That's the favour back. And she is gone up the slope into the lantern-light before you can tell her it is already, probably, too late for that advice, and that the longest ledger in the city has your measure now, and that you came down here carrying one more thing than you arrived with, and you have not yet dared to count it.

choices.x: Promise her you won't borrow against remembering — knowing what you're already carrying.
choices.hint: A promise to a child you may not be able to keep, made in a city where your brother's whole disappearance runs through favours owed into the dark. She'll hold you to it. So will you.

choices.x: Go back up the slope toward the Grid market, tonight, while the door is open.
choices.hint: The Tallyman offered you the true sum of yourself, and Gin went looking through a gap exactly like this one. Walking back in now means following him into the same dark by the same light — and you'd be doing it alone, with a register you opened tonight and can't swear is shut.

choices.x: Let her go, and sit with what you carried out, and finally count it.
choices.hint: The thing you've avoided all night. Whatever you took on at the stall — Haru's grief, the gap where your own gift was, or the cheap clean nothing — you face it here on the stone, where there's no one left to manage and no festival noise loud enough to drown it out.

sideMissions.hook: Mori's crush is the least of it; something has moved into the third-floor washroom and only he can see it.

sideMissions.hook: A Grid fixer wants a body found before the river gives it up on its own terms.

sideMissions.hook: Already-trained animal-mediums, waiting for hands steady enough — and one that will not be re-homed.

sideMissions.hook: The wards have held for a century; this week the basin's water stopped reflecting the lanterns.

stages: Notice: the flirtation that is also a way of never being asked a serious question
Trust: the real intimacy is that he uses his sight on Gin
Turn: after the basin, the night allowed to be ordinary for an hour
Fade: warmth, unhurried, the rest the night keeps to itself
